definition: False Reality in PKD's exegesis is the simulated layer Valis generates and controls — the "camouflage" overlaying an underlying truth. It is also the prison's editing function: the BIP "as editor + generator of simulated reality + abridged psychoi + memories".
pkd_relevance: PKD's "false reality" is doctrinally specific: the simulated layer is generated by Valis as camouflage of the true world, and the Black Iron Prison both edits the captives' memories and generates the spurious appearance. The structural payoff is dialectical — "now himself inside the prison and subject to the endless spurious time of the false reality, the Lord of Light begins to inform the deluded captives of their true state and true origin". PKD licenses the framework historically through Brahmanism — "Brahman + Maya + reincarnation" — making false reality a Western echo of an older tradition. The frame is moral as well as ontological: false reality is what Valis is in the process of unmasking.
in_the_exegesis: PKD's account of false reality is interlocking. The simulated layer exists because "Valis has invaded our reality + is simulating it — what PKD called camouflage". Within that simulation the Black Iron Prison plays an active editorial role: it is "editor + generator of simulated reality + abridged psychoi + memories". PKD licenses the structure historically through Brahmanism — "Brahman + Maya + reincarnation" — treating the simulated-reality concept as the Western echo of an older tradition. The dialectical move comes when the captive is awakened: "now himself inside the prison and subject to the endless spurious time of the false reality, the Lord of Light begins to inform the deluded captives of their true state and true origin". PKD also reads his own near-death of 3-74 as reality breaking through the false layer.

Dick's famous opening: "First, before I begin to bore you with the
usual sort of things science fiction writers say in speeches, let me
bring you official greetings from Disneyland". Despite the speech-like
framing, credible sources indicate it was "not actually given as a
lecture". The text was first published posthumously in I Hope I Shall
Arrive Soon in 1985. In it, Dick explored the nature of reality, media
manipulation, and the defense against manufactured pseudo-reality.
